title: Third reason: what may never be remitted may justly be forever punished—even in the just, absolutely speaking
source_text: LXVI. Tertio peccata quae dicuntur venialia, ex se poenam aeternam mereri sic probatur, Quod potest nunquam remitti, potest in aeternum puniri, idque juste. Peccata autem quaevis, etiam levissima, in quacunque tandem persona reperiantur, ab-solute loquendo, possent nunquam remitti: quoniam peccatum quodvis, quum a Deo remittitur, ex misericordia & gratia remittitur; quod importat ipsum nomen remis-sionis. Quicquid autem Deus ex gratia & misericordia facit, id simpliciter & absolute loquendo, posset non facere: & proinde ipsis justis, simpliciter loquendo, & sine respectu ad promissiones in Evangelio gratuito factas, posset Deus ipsa levissima peccata non remittere, adeoque illa in aeternum punire.
pass_a_gloss: Thirdly, that sins which are called venial of themselves merit eternal punishment is proved thus: What can never be remitted can be forever punished, and that justly. But any sins, even the lightest, in whatever person finally they are found, absolutely speaking, could never be remitted: since any sin, when it is remitted by God, is remitted from mercy and grace; which the very name of remission imports. But whatever God does from grace and mercy, that simply and absolutely speaking he could not do: and therefore even to the just, simply speaking and without respect to the promises freely made in the Gospel, God could not remit the very lightest sins, and so could punish them forever.
pass_b_english: Remission is mercy by definition—so absolutely, even for the just, God could withhold pardon of the lightest faults and punish them forever.
